titles.Mucosa: Connective tissue, small vessels and muscularis mucosae
titles.Submucosa: Connective tissue, vessels and nerve plexus

Epithelium.description: The colon is lined by a single layer of tall absorptive cells (colonocytes) interspersed with many mucus-secreting goblet cells. It has no villi, so the surface is flat and pitted by the openings of straight crypts, where stem cells at the base constantly replace the lining.
clinical: Most colorectal cancers develop from adenomatous polyps in this lining. Loss of the APC gene is usually an early step, which switches on Wnt signalling in the crypt cells.

Mucosa.description: The lamina propria is the loose connective tissue packed between the crypts, rich in immune cells and capillaries. Arterioles and venules run through it, and the thin muscularis mucosae at its base separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
clinical: In ulcerative colitis, inflammation is confined to the mucosa and usually starts in the rectum, spreading continuously upward. The lamina propria fills with neutrophils and plasma cells, and neutrophils that invade the crypts form crypt abscesses.
Solitary lymphoid follicles in the colon are normal parts of the gut immune system, but they can swell (lymphoid hyperplasia) during infection.
The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is also missing from the aganglionic distal segment in Hirschsprung disease, so that part of the bowel cannot relax and the bowel above it dilates.

Muscularis externa.description: The muscle coat of the colon wall has two layers. The inner circular layer narrows the lumen, while the outer longitudinal layer shortens the colon and is gathered into three bands, the taeniae coli. The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, a network of nerve ganglia, lies between the two layers and coordinates their contractions.
clinical: Diverticula (pouches) form where the mucosa and submucosa bulge outward through weak spots in the muscle coat where blood vessels pierce it, most often in the sigmoid colon.

In Hirschsprung disease the distal bowel lacks ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, so this segment cannot relax and the bowel above it dilates; it often presents in newborns with delayed passage of meconium.
Perforation of the colon, for example from diverticulitis or a tumour, lets faeces spill into the peritoneal cavity, which this serosa lines, and causes peritonitis.

Cell detail (8×).description: This close-up shows the cells of the colon wall at 8 times magnification. Colonocytes and goblet cells rest on a basement membrane, beneath which lie the lamina propria's fibroblasts, capillaries and red blood cells. In a goblet cell the nucleus is pushed down to the broad base, and the upper cell is filled with a rounded mucin mass made of granules about 1 micrometre across.

parts.description: Surface colonocytes are the tall, simple columnar absorptive cells that form the luminal surface of the colon between the openings of the crypts. Like crypt colonocytes, they carry a brush border of microvilli and absorb water and salts from the luminal contents, and they are shed into the lumen and replaced from the crypts below. In a section, the surface appears as a continuous sheet of columnar cells with oval nuclei near their bases, interrupted only by the crypt openings.

Goblet cells are mucus-secreting epithelial cells scattered among the absorptive colonocytes, and they are far more numerous in the colon than in the small intestine. Each cell is flask-shaped, with a narrow base resting on the basement membrane and a broad apex packed with mucin. In routine haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) sections the mucin is largely lost during processing, so the apex looks pale and empty and the nucleus is pushed down into the base, which is the easiest way to pick these cells out among the colonocytes.

Goblet cell mucin is the secretory product stored as granules in the apical part of each goblet cell. Mucins are large, heavily sugar-coated proteins (glycoproteins) that absorb water to form a slippery, viscous gel. This mucus coats the colonic surface and lubricates the passage of the faeces as they become more solid. Special stains show it clearly: periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains neutral mucins magenta and Alcian blue stains acidic mucins blue.

Crypt stem cells are the undifferentiated cells at the base of each colonic crypt, and they divide to renew the epithelium every few days. Their daughter cells move up the crypt wall and mature into absorptive colonocytes and goblet cells. In a section they are small, plain columnar cells, recognised by their position in the lowest part of the crypt, where cell division (mitosis) is most frequent. Paneth cells, which support stem cells in the small intestine, are normally absent from the distal colon.

The brush border is the dense fringe of microvilli on the free (luminal) surface of the absorptive colonocytes. Each microvillus is a finger-like extension of the cell membrane, strengthened by a core of actin filaments, that greatly increases the surface area available for absorbing water and salts. In routine sections the brush border shows as a fine, pink-staining, striated band at the luminal edge of the cells, and in the colon it is shorter and less dense than in the small intestine.

Epithelial nuclei are the nuclei of the simple columnar cells that line the colon, both the absorptive colonocytes and the goblet cells. In colonocytes the oval nuclei sit towards the base of the cell, whereas in a goblet cell the nucleus is pushed down into the narrow base beneath the mucin. Seen together in a section, they form a single, neatly spaced row of dark nuclei along the base of the epithelium, which confirms that the lining is one layer of cells.

The lamina propria is the loose connective tissue of the mucosa that fills the spaces between the crypts and supports the epithelium. It lies between the epithelium above and the muscularis mucosae below, and it contains fibroblasts, a rich capillary network and many lymphocytes and plasma cells that defend the gut. In a section it is the pale, finely fibrous, cellular tissue between the crypt tubes, recognised by its many small dark nuclei.

Lamina propria immune cells are the lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, eosinophils and mast cells that are found in the connective tissue of the mucosa. Plasma cells are the most numerous of these, and they secrete immunoglobulin A (IgA) into the gut lumen, where it helps neutralise microbes without triggering inflammation. In a section they appear as small, dark, round nuclei scattered through the pale connective tissue, and plasma cells can be recognised by their eccentric, clock-face chromatin.

The pericryptal capillary network is the dense mesh of fine capillaries that surrounds each colonic crypt in the lamina propria. Branches from the arterioles at the crypt base climb the crypt wall and form a ring beneath the surface epithelium, supplying oxygen and nutrients and draining absorbed products. In a section it appears as many small, thin-walled vessels containing red blood cells, packed around the crypt tubes.

Mucosal arterioles are the small muscular arteries that carry blood up from the submucosa, through the muscularis mucosae, and into the mucosa to feed the capillary network around each crypt. Their wall has a thick ring of smooth muscle around a small lumen, which lets them adjust blood flow. In a section they are recognised by that thicker muscular wall, and they usually lie alongside the thin-walled mucosal venules.

Mucosal venules are the small, thin-walled veins of the mucosa that collect blood from the capillary network around the crypts and carry it down between the crypts towards the submucosal veins. Their walls contain very little smooth muscle, so they are more easily collapsed and irregular than the arterioles. In a section they appear as thin-walled vessels with a wide lumen, usually lying beside the arterioles.

The muscularis mucosae is the thin layer of smooth muscle at the base of the mucosa, lying between the lamina propria and the submucosa. Its contraction wrinkles the mucosal surface and helps to empty the crypts. In a section it is a narrow band of spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells with elongated nuclei, lying just beneath the crypt bases, and it is pierced in places by vessels and lymphoid follicles.

The mantle zone is the outer ring of densely packed small lymphocytes, mostly resting B cells, that surrounds the germinal centre of a lymphoid follicle. The follicle is part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT), the immune tissue of the gut wall, and in the colon the follicles are usually solitary nodules that lie in the mucosa and can extend down into the submucosa. In a section the mantle zone is a crown of dark, small, round nuclei, tightly packed compared with the paler germinal centre it surrounds.

The germinal centre is the central zone of a lymphoid follicle, where activated B lymphocytes (antibody-making cells) multiply rapidly. Here the B cells mutate their antibody genes (somatic hypermutation) and switch antibody class, and those with high-affinity antibodies are selected with help from follicular dendritic cells (antigen-displaying cells) and T helper cells (T lymphocytes that help B cells). In a section it is paler and less densely packed than the surrounding mantle, with larger B cell nuclei and scattered tingible body macrophages (phagocytes that clear dead cells).

Lymphocyte nuclei are the nuclei of the small lymphocytes, mainly B cells, that fill a lymphoid follicle. In the mantle zone they are small, round, dark and tightly packed, whereas in the germinal centre the nuclei are larger, paler and more widely spaced, because they belong to the proliferating B cells there. This crowding is what sets the follicle apart from the looser, more varied cells of the surrounding lamina propria.

The submucosa is the layer of dense irregular connective tissue between the muscularis mucosae and the inner circular muscle, binding the mucosa to the muscle coat. It carries the larger blood and lymphatic vessels and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, and it contains scattered fat cells in a meshwork of collagen fibres. In a section it looks dense and fibrous. Unlike the duodenum, the colon has no Brunner glands, which are mucus-secreting glands found in the duodenal submucosa.

Submucosal arterioles are the small muscular arteries of the submucosa that carry blood from the larger arteries towards the mucosa and the muscle coats. Their wall has a thick ring of smooth muscle around a small, round lumen, which lets them adjust the blood supply to the gut wall. In a section they are recognised by that thick muscular wall, and they usually lie beside the thin-walled submucosal venules.

Submucosal venules are the thin-walled small veins of the submucosa that collect blood draining from the mucosa and the muscle layers and carry it into the larger submucosal veins. Their walls contain little smooth muscle, so their lumens are wide and their outline is often irregular or collapsed. In a section they are recognised by these thin walls and open lumens, and they usually sit alongside the thicker-walled submucosal arterioles.

The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is a network of nerve ganglia and fibres lying in the submucosa, between the inner circular muscle and the mucosa. It is part of the enteric nervous system, which controls the gut largely without input from the brain, and it regulates local secretion, absorption and blood flow. In a section it appears as small clusters of ganglion cells, each with a large, pale nucleus and a prominent nucleolus, joined by fine nerve strands.

The inner circular muscle is the inner of the two smooth muscle layers of the muscularis externa, lying between the submucosa and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus. Its fibres wrap around the bowel, so when they contract they narrow the lumen and help propel the contents along. In a transverse section the circular fibres run along the plane of the cut, so they appear as a band of long, parallel, spindle-shaped cells, whereas the outer longitudinal layer appears as small, round profiles.

Circular muscle nuclei are the nuclei of the smooth muscle cells in the inner circular layer of the muscularis externa. Each smooth muscle cell has a single, long, cigar-shaped nucleus near its centre, and because the fibres run around the bowel, these nuclei look like long, parallel, spindle-shaped profiles. They are longer than the rounder, paler nuclei of the nerve cells in the neighbouring plexuses, which helps you recognise the muscle layer.

The myenteric connective septum is the thin layer of loose connective tissue lying between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle coats of the muscularis externa. It holds the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, together with small blood vessels and nerve fibres that supply both muscle layers. In a section, look for a pale, slightly loose band of connective tissue containing small clusters of nerve cells, separating the two muscle layers.

The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus is a network of ganglia (small clusters of nerve cell bodies) and nerve fibres lying between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layers of the gut wall. It is the main controller of gut motility, regulating the strength and coordination of the contractions that drive peristalsis, the wave-like movement that moves food along the bowel. Under the microscope, look for small clusters of large nerve cells lying in the connective tissue between the two muscle layers.

Myenteric ganglion neurons are the nerve cell bodies that make up the ganglia of the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus. They include motor neurons that stimulate or inhibit the smooth muscle, and interneurons that link them together to run the gut's local reflexes. Under the microscope the cell bodies are large, with abundant cytoplasm, so they look bigger than the surrounding smooth muscle cells.

Myenteric neuron nuclei are the nuclei of the enteric nerve cells in the myenteric plexus. They are large, round and pale, with fine, open chromatin and a visible nucleolus, unlike the small, dense nuclei of the surrounding smooth muscle. Recognising them in a section helps you locate the ganglia of the plexus between the two muscle layers.

keys: Outer longitudinal muscle and taenia coli
parts.description: The outer longitudinal muscle is the outer smooth muscle coat of the muscularis externa, lying beneath the serosa and running along the bowel. In the colon most of its fibres are gathered into three thickened bands, the taeniae coli, with only a thin layer between them; these bands shorten the bowel and pull it into pouches called haustra. In a transverse section the longitudinal fibres are cut end-on as small round profiles, outside the inner circular layer, whose fibres run around the bowel and look elongated.

Longitudinal muscle nuclei are the nuclei of the smooth muscle cells in the outer longitudinal layer, including those in the taeniae coli. Each smooth muscle cell has a single, elongated nucleus lying near its centre. Where the fibres are seen end-on in a transverse section, their nuclei appear as small, round, dense dots, quite unlike the large, pale nuclei of the myenteric neurons.

The serosal connective tissue is the thin layer of loose connective tissue that lies directly beneath the mesothelium on the outer surface of the colon. It carries small blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerve fibres to the outer muscle coat, and it firmly binds the surface mesothelium to the muscle beneath. In a section, it appears as a narrow band of collagen fibres and scattered fibroblasts between the mesothelium and the outer longitudinal muscle.

The mesothelium is the single layer of flat, scale-like (squamous) cells that forms the smooth outer surface of the bowel, as part of the visceral peritoneum. Its cells are thin and flattened and secrete a small amount of watery fluid, which lets the bowel glide against neighbouring organs with little friction. Look for a delicate, continuous line of thin cells along the outermost edge of the tissue.

Mesothelial nuclei are the flattened, oval nuclei of the squamous mesothelial cells that line the outer surface of the bowel. Because the cells are so thin, each nucleus bulges up from the cell surface, so the nuclei show as small, flattened ovals spaced along the outer edge of the section. Spotting them along the outermost edge is a useful clue for recognising the serosa under the microscope.

Colonocytes are the tall, column-shaped absorptive cells that make up most of the lining of the colon, on both the surface and within the crypts (the tubular glands that open onto the surface). They absorb water and electrolytes, especially sodium, from the bowel contents and pass them into the blood. Each cell has a brush border of microvilli facing the lumen and an oval nucleus near its base, and goblet cells are scattered among them.

Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells scattered among the colonocytes (the absorptive lining cells) of the surface and crypt epithelium. They are flask-shaped, with a narrow base holding a small, dark, flattened nucleus that is pushed to the bottom of the cell, and a broad apex distended with mucin. In a section, look for a clear, bubble-like cell among the columnar lining cells; their mucus lubricates the bowel contents and protects the lining.

Goblet cell mucin is the mucus stored in the theca, the broad, cup-shaped upper part of a goblet cell. Mucins are large glycoproteins, heavily sugar-coated proteins that form a slippery gel which lubricates the bowel contents and protects the lining from digestive enzymes and abrasion. In H&E sections mucin stains poorly, so the theca usually looks pale or empty.

Mucin secretory granules (mucinogen granules) are the membrane-bound vesicles that store mucin inside a goblet cell until the cell releases it. Each granule holds condensed mucin and fuses with the apical cell membrane to empty its contents into the lumen by exocytosis. Individual granules are resolved only by electron microscopy; with the light microscope they merge into the pale theca.

Epithelial nuclei are the nuclei of the colonocytes (the absorptive lining cells) and goblet cells that form the lining of the colon. In the absorptive cells they are oval and lie in a neat row near the base of each cell, while goblet cell nuclei are flattened and pushed down to the narrow base. They stain strongly with haematoxylin, so they show as dark ovals across the lining.

The brush border is the dense fringe of microvilli on the free (luminal) surface of the colonocytes (the absorptive lining cells), facing into the gut lumen. Each microvillus is a tiny finger-like extension of the cell membrane, supported by a bundle of actin filaments, and together they greatly increase the surface area available for absorbing water and electrolytes. In a section, the brush border shows as a fine, pink, striated band along the luminal edge of the epithelium.

The basement membrane is a thin, specialised sheet of extracellular matrix that separates the colonic epithelium from the lamina propria beneath it. It is made mainly of type IV collagen and laminin, secreted largely by the epithelial cells, and it anchors the epithelium while acting as a selective filter between the two layers. In routine H&E sections it is very thin and easy to miss, but a periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain colours it magenta, making it visible.

The lamina propria (Latin for 'own layer') is the loose connective tissue lying directly beneath the colonic epithelium, filling the space between the crypts and the muscularis mucosae. It supports the epithelium and houses fibroblasts, capillaries, lymphocytes, plasma cells and other immune cells that defend the gut lining. Under the microscope it is the pale, loosely packed tissue between the crypt tubes, scattered with round cells and small blood vessels.

The capillary wall is the single layer of thin endothelial (lining) cells, resting on a basement membrane, that forms the wall of the smallest blood vessels, the capillaries. This wall lets oxygen, nutrients and absorbed fluid pass between the blood and the surrounding tissue, and capillaries form a dense network beneath the crypts. In a section, look for a tiny, round vessel whose flattened endothelial nuclei bulge into a lumen containing red blood cells.

Red blood cells (erythrocytes) are small, anucleate (lacking a nucleus), biconcave discs that carry oxygen bound to haemoglobin and help carry carbon dioxide back to the lungs. They travel through the capillaries and small venules of the lamina propria, delivering oxygen to the colonic mucosa. In a stained section they appear as bright pink discs with a pale centre and no nucleus.

Fibroblasts are the connective tissue cells of the lamina propria that make the collagen, reticular fibres and ground substance forming the supporting framework of the mucosa. They are spindle-shaped, with long, slender processes that extend between neighbouring cells and the fibres. Look for an elongated, lightly stained cell with a thin, pale nucleus lying among the collagen fibres, away from the dense epithelium.

The fibroblast nucleus is the elongated, oval nucleus of a fibroblast in the lamina propria. Its chromatin is fine and pale, so it looks lighter than the dense nuclei of lymphocytes and smooth muscle, and its shape follows the spindle-shaped cell it sits in. Recognising these nuclei helps you tell loose connective tissue apart from the crowded epithelium above.
